status_summary: DOJ has changed course on both strands as of October 2026. For the FACE Act, DOJ's Office of the Pardon Attorney records a full and unconditional pardon on 2025-01-23 of 24 individuals convicted or charged in five cases (NPR reported 23 people), NPR reported three pending cases were dropped, and DOJ said it would bring abortion-related FACE Act actions only in extraordinary circumstances, such as cases involving death or serious property damage; DOJ has continued to use the Act at houses of worship, filing a civil suit over a New Jersey synagogue protest (2025-09-29) and a superseding indictment against 39 defendants over a St. Paul church protest (2026-02-27). On consent decrees, Attorney General Bondi's memoranda of 2025-02-05 reinstated the prohibition on improper third-party settlements (rescinding the May 2022 guidelines and a July 2023 environmental division memo) and directed components to review consent decrees and settlement agreements, grants and contracts for race- or sex-based preferences and DEI criteria, without taking action that may violate a court order or decree before consulting the Office of Legal Counsel. On 2025-05-21 DOJ moved to dismiss its Louisville police suit and to quash a proposed Minneapolis decree; both were proposed decrees that no federal judge had approved, and DOJ also planned to drop six police investigations (NPR, via WFAE). On 2026-09-24 DOJ announced it was ending more than 50 school desegregation cases through case-by-case review in which it seeks dismissal once it concludes a district has achieved unitary status; DOJ's release describes them as outdated consent decrees. Separately, DOJ announced on 2025-11-19 and 2025-11-21 that federal courts terminated the New Orleans (2013) and Newark (2016) police consent decrees on motions DOJ joined or supported.

timeline.event: The President grants full and unconditional pardons to 24 unique individuals in five cases involving clinic-access offenses (DOJ Office of the Pardon Attorney; the warrant lists case captions, not offenses, and contains no direction to dismiss pending cases); NPR reports 23 pardons, three dropped cases, and a DOJ charging policy limiting new abortion-related FACE Act actions to rare circumstances (the policy date of 2025-01-24 is per a Wikipedia summary).

timeline.event: Attorney General Bondi issues memoranda including 'Reinstating the Prohibition on Improper Third-Party Settlements' (settlements should not direct payments to non-governmental organizations that were neither victims nor parties, except in limited circumstances; rescinds the May 2022 guidelines and a July 2023 environmental division memo; the Associate Attorney General reports within 30 days) and 'Eliminating Internal Discriminatory Practices' (components review consent decrees and settlement agreements, grants and contracts for race- or sex-based preferences and DEI criteria, and consult the Office of Legal Counsel before acting contrary to a court order or decree). Lawfare also describes a Weaponization Working Group whose review includes prosecutions of anti-abortion activists.

DOJ moves to dismiss its Louisville police suit (ending a proposed, unapproved consent decree) and to quash a proposed Minneapolis decree, and says it will drop six police investigations including Memphis and Phoenix.
DOJ files a civil FACE Act suit in the District of New Jersey over a November 2024 protest at a West Orange synagogue, seeking an injunction.
A federal court terminates the 2013 New Orleans Police Department consent decree on a joint motion by DOJ and the city.
A federal court terminates the 2016 Newark Police Department consent decree on the city's motion, which DOJ supported.

DOJ announces 30 additional defendants, bringing the total to 39, in a District of Minnesota case over a protest at a St. Paul church, charged with a FACE Act misdemeanor and a felony conspiracy count; defendants have pleaded not guilty and a magistrate judge earlier rejected some warrants.
DOJ announces it is ending more than 50 school desegregation cases from the 1960s and 1970s through a case-by-case review, seeking dismissal once a district has achieved unitary status.
